\chapter{Asking Someone's Age}
\label{ch:hi-asking-age}

\section[\hi{उम्र}]{\hi{उम्र} — the same word as Arabic}

\label{lesson:HI-C19-umr}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} You just met Arabic's \emph{ʿumr}. Hindi's everyday word for "age" is the \textbf{exact same word}, carried through Persian.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — \hi{उम्र} — a Perso-Arabic loan, and a native alternative}
\textbf{\hi{उम्र}} (\emph{umr}) = "\textbf{age}" — this is \textbf{Arabic's ʿumr}, borrowed into Hindi through Persian, and it's the everyday, colloquial word most Hindi speakers use. Hindi also has a fully \textbf{native Sanskrit} alternative, \textbf{\hi{आयु}} (\emph{āyu}, "age, lifespan"), which feels more formal or literary — a register split you've now seen several times (compare Kannada's Sanskrit-tatsama \emph{madhyāhna} vs. Tamil's native words for the same concepts, just flipped here: the \textbf{borrowed} word is the everyday one, the \textbf{native} word is the formal one).

\subsection*{Guided Practice}
{[}PAUSE 1s{]}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "umr" — age, same word as Arabic's ʿumr{]}
  \item {[}YOU CONTRAST: everyday \emph{umr} · formal/literary \emph{āyu}{]}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Wrap-up recall}]
{[}PAUSE 3s{]} What language does Hindi's \textbf{\hi{उम्र}} come from, and what's the native Sanskrit alternative? (\textbf{Arabic} \emph{ʿumr}, via Persian; native alternative is \textbf{\hi{आयु}}, \emph{āyu}.) Which one is ordinary conversational Hindi? (\textbf{Umr}.) Next: use a genitive marker to say how many years someone belongs to.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kitne sāl ke ho?]{\hi{कितने} \hi{साल} \hi{के} \hi{हो}? — belonging to so many years}

\label{lesson:HI-C19-age-grammar}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} Languages do not agree on whether age is something you have, are, were born with, or state without a verb. Hindi gives the idea a fifth shape.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — The two sentences}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\hi{तुम} \hi{कितने} \hi{साल} \hi{के} \hi{हो}?} — "How old are you?" (informal), literally "you, \textbf{of how many years, are}?" (\emph{tum kitne sāl ke ho?})
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\hi{मैं} \hi{बीस} \hi{साल} \hi{का} \hi{हूँ।}} — "I am twenty years old," literally "I {[}am one{]} \textbf{belonging to twenty years}." (\emph{maiṅ bīs sāl kā hūṅ.})
\end{quote}

\textbf{\hi{के}/\hi{का}} (\emph{ke/kā}) is Hindi's \textbf{genitive postposition}, "of, belonging to." The same marker family handles possession elsewhere: \emph{merā ghar}, "my house."

So Hindi does not copy Romance's "I \textbf{have} years," Germanic's simple "I \textbf{am} {[}a number{]}," Latin's "\textbf{born} + N years," or Arabic's verbless "my age {[}is{]} N." It says "I am {[}one{]} \textbf{belonging to} N years," with a genitive marker plus \textbf{\hi{होना}} (\emph{honā}, "to be").

\subsection*{Guided Practice}
{[}PAUSE 1s{]}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "tum kitne sāl ke ho?" — how old are you?{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "maiṅ bīs sāl kā hūṅ" — I belong to twenty years{]}
  \item {[}YOU POINT: \textbf{ke/kā} — the genitive, "of/belonging to"{]}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Wrap-up recall}]
{[}PAUSE 3s{]} What does \textbf{\hi{के}/\hi{का}} mark? (A \textbf{genitive/possessive} relationship.) Does Hindi use Romance "have," simple Germanic "be," Latin "born," or Arabic's verbless sentence? (\textbf{None}: it says "belonging to N years" + \emph{honā}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
